# The Center of the World

In Hereford Cathedral they keep a room deliberately dark, because what's in it is fragile, and old, and does not take light well. It is a map of the world, drawn around the year 1300 on a single calfskin: the largest medieval world map to survive, nearly five feet tall, dense with ink and gold. The unknown draftsman put east at the top, because that's where the sun rises and where Eden was understood to sit. Christ reigns at the summit. Jerusalem occupies the exact center. Britain, where the map was actually made, is squeezed into the far-left margin like an afterthought. Noah's Ark rests on Ararat. The labyrinth of Crete coils in the Aegean. The Golden Fleece hangs in the Caucasus. And off in the south, in the margins of Africa, the monsters. The map very nearly left the cathedral in the 1980s, when a proposed sale to fund repairs caused a public outcry, and it was the outcry that kept it: a small mercy, since it's hard to think of a stranger object to lose.

The modern viewer's first instinct is to call it wrong. But "wrong" assumes it was attempting what our maps attempt and failing at it. It wasn't. It's a different genre entirely: an encyclopedia in the shape of the world, a sermon in the shape of the world. It doesn't measure miles; it measures importance. Places are drawn large because they matter. In that sense it is more honest than most maps we use, because its values are printed right on its surface, in gold, at the top. Even the word is humble about all this. *Mappa* meant cloth, napkin. The world, drawn on something the size of a tablecloth, at the scale of one family's dinner.

---

All maps are arguments. Every map is a set of claims about what matters, and the louder claim is always about what doesn't: what got left out so the rest could be legible. The modern map hides its editorial hand behind the grid of latitude and longitude and the reassuring beige of continents, but the hand is there. Selection is not a defect that better technology will remove. The only map with no editorial hand is the territory itself, and it is useless as a map. An essay, for that matter, is just a map with opinions.

Lewis Carroll saw the problem early. In *Sylvie and Bruno Concluded*, a character boasts of his kingdom's map at a scale of a mile to a mile. The farmers object that it would cover the whole country and shut out the sunlight, so it is never spread out. Borges compressed the joke into a single paragraph, "On Exactitude in Science": an empire of perfect cartographers produces a map the size of the empire, point for point coincident with it, and later generations, less devoted, abandon it to the sun and the rain. Cartography is the art of leaving things out. A good map is a betrayal so skillful you're grateful for it.

---

You cannot flatten a sphere without lying. Geometry itself forbids it: the curvature of the earth cannot be pressed into a plane without something tearing or stretching. So every flat map chooses which truth to keep and which to abandon: area, shape, distance, or direction. Pick one. There is no arrangement of the choices that avoids a lie; there are only different lies for different jobs.

Gerardus Mercator, in 1569, picked direction, because his customers were drowning. On a Mercator map, a line of constant compass bearing (the line a ship actually holds when the helmsman keeps the needle steady) is straight. A navigator could put a ruler on the chart, draw a line from the Azores to the Caribbean, and steer it home. For this mercy, the poles swell grotesquely: to keep the bearings honest, the map must stretch the top of the world like taffy, which is why Greenland, a rough subcontinental icebox, looms on the classroom wall like a rival to Africa, a continent about fourteen times its size.

The projection was built for the North Atlantic, and it flattered the North Atlantic. Then it escaped the ship and colonized the schoolroom, where its one talent, steering, was worthless and its distortion was dynamite. Generations of children absorbed the relative size of nations from it, the way you absorb fluoride, without noticing. The reckoning came in the 1970s, when Arno Peters promoted an equal-area projection as a corrective to centuries of visual inflation and deflation; development agencies hung it in their lobbies, professional cartographers grumbled that his map mangled shapes and his history was shaky (the argument even got a scene in *The West Wing*), and the fight grew loud and moral and largely missed the point. The point is that every projection is a choice among lies. The only innocent map is a globe, and you can't fold a globe, file it, or hang it on a classroom wall. Convenience corrupts everything, including up. North-up is a habit, not a fact; an Australian named Stuart McArthur made this point in 1979 with his upside-down world map, Australia crowning the planet, and no one has produced an argument against it except habit.

---

Before maps were advertisements, they were armaments. In the sixteenth century the Portuguese crown treated its rutters and charts as secrets of the highest order: captains received them before a voyage and were expected to surrender them after, and leaking one abroad was treated as a species of treason. To hold an accurate chart of a coast was to own that coast's future; every rival hull would have to rediscover, the hard way, the reefs you already knew. Then a curious reversal. In the 1840s and '50s, an American naval officer named Matthew Fontaine Maury, stuck on shore by an old leg injury, got the idea of mining the thousands of dusty ship logs in the navy's archives for their weather observations, and out of them compiled wind and current charts that shortened ocean passages by weeks. He refused to keep them national. He wrote to every maritime flag on earth asking for logbooks, the logbooks came back, and the world's sailors ended up sharing one map. It was arguably the first great international open-science project, and it began with a lame officer in a dim room reading other people's diaries.

Maps don't merely describe power; sometimes they are the instrument of it. In 1930s America, federal appraisers drew maps of cities and graded the neighborhoods, and the worst grade, shaded in red, was assigned where Black and immigrant families lived and labeled "hazardous." Lenders steered capital around those districts for decades, and the decline the map predicted, its readers did much to produce. Red ink hardened into fact, into walls, into a geography of exclusion whose lines are still visible from above, in tree cover and life expectancy and property values, in nearly any American city you care to check. This is the uncomfortable energy in the word "cartography" that Maury's story partly redeems: naming a coast has always been a way of claiming it, and drawing a line has always been a way of making one.

---

In 1933, London's Underground published a map designed by Harry Beck, an engineering draftsman who happened at the time to be out of work. Beck's insight was ruthless: nobody uses the Underground map to walk. A passenger needs to know sequence and interchange, not geography. So he threw geography away. Stations spaced evenly no matter the actual distance. Lines restricted to horizontals, verticals, and forty-five-degree diagonals. The Thames reduced to a single blue gesture. The story goes that he took the logic from electrical circuit diagrams, which don't care where the components physically sit either. The design was initially rejected, then tried in a pocket edition, and within a few years it was the mental furniture of an entire city, and then of every city: nearly every metro diagram on earth, from Tokyo to Moscow to your phone, is one of Beck's children.

The city rearranged itself to match the diagram. Distances stretched and shrank in the popular imagination: central stations a few hundred meters apart look like expeditions, and tourists take taxis between them, while long suburban runs look like nothing at all. People chose flats by diagram logic. The map ate the territory. And Beck himself received a modest one-time fee, then spent four decades submitting revisions while others signed the work; recognition arrived mostly after his death. It is among the most-seen British designs of the twentieth century, and its author spent much of his life trying to get his name back on it, which tells you something about how maps treat their makers, too.

---

For most of history, being on a map was an achievement reserved for cities, rivers, coastlines, and kings. People lived in the spaces between the labels. Now the average person spends the entire day as a moving blue point. The map no longer asks where you are; it tells you. An entire genre of small civic performance, the fingertip on the folded paper, the "you are here" sign at the trailhead, the stranger stopped on the corner and consulted like an oracle, has nearly gone extinct.

The new maps argue in subtler voices. Open a map of Crimea in Moscow and the peninsula is solidly Russian; open it in Washington and it's dashed, contested, a question mark. One body of water carries different names depending on the nationality of your internet connection. In 2018 the fitness app Strava published a global heat map of its users' runs and rides, and analysts noticed bright rings of athletic activity around certain compounds in certain deserts, where soldiers had been jogging with their trackers on: a map of exercise became a map of secret infrastructure. And every time your phone hands you the "fastest route," someone's algorithm is deciding which streets deserve your presence, which shuttered storefronts you'll pass, which neighborhoods you will never see at all. We asked for the whole world in our pockets. What we got is a very persuasive opinion about it.

There's also this: we have nearly abolished getting lost. It used to be a distinct state of being, with its own physiology (the tightening stomach, the slow panic) and its own literature; Odysseus spends ten years lost, and it's the best part of the book. Lostness had products: the accidental neighborhood discovered while wrong about everything, the diner found at the exact moment of despair. Nobody misses being lost at night in a strange city, least of all anyone who has been lost at night in a strange city and had reason to fear it. But serendipity was lostness's byproduct, and the optimized route is a machine with no byproducts. The fastest way to get anywhere is, by definition, a way that passes through nothing.

---

The maps that matter most are unpublished. In 1960 the urban planner Kevin Lynch asked people in Boston, Jersey City, and Los Angeles to sketch their cities from memory, and out of the wobbly, contradictory drawings he extracted the five elements of every mental map: paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks. Everyone's map is wrong in informative ways. Home is enormous. The commute is a trunk line, wide as a river. The district two miles away is blank as the open sea.

Ask someone for directions and you receive a fragment of autobiography. "Left where the video store used to be." "Past the good bakery, not the disappointing one." We navigate by demolished buildings. Our mental maps are of time as much as space, layered palimpsests of every place we've lived, and the person giving directions is reading from a map no one else can see, of a city that partially no longer exists. As for "here be dragons": the phrase, famously, appears essentially once in the entire history of cartography, on a small copper globe from around 1510 now in the New York Public Library. But the condition it names is real, and everyone has one: unexplored water inside the harbor, the neighborhood five miles from your door that you have never once entered, though you have flown over other continents.

Some evidence that the mental map is a real organ: London's black-cab drivers must master "the Knowledge," years spent memorizing every street and permissible route in a vast city, and brain scans of those who complete it show a measurably enlarged posterior hippocampus, the region that handles spatial memory. The map grows in the head, like a muscle. The corollary is less cheerful: early studies of people navigating by GPS find less of that same structure lighting up at all, the device taking the load the way an elevator takes the load of stairs. Convenience is a fine thing. So is a hippocampus. The mind, like the city, becomes what we practice.

Not all maps even map land. The navigators of the Marshall Islands made charts of sticks and cowrie shells, the curved sticks representing the way ocean swells bend and interfere around atolls, the shells marking the islands themselves: maps not of where things are but of how the sea behaves. And many of these charts were meant to be memorized and then left on shore. Their success was measured by how completely you could stop needing them. That is the exact opposite of the blue dot, which never lets you graduate.

---

Some things are still blank. Only about a quarter of the ocean floor has been mapped to modern resolution; we have better maps of Mars, and of the Moon, than of most of our own planet's surface. The nearest alien world is under the keel. There is an effort underway, Seabed 2030, to finish the job, and it should be finished. But it's worth noticing what a blank used to be. *Terra Australis Incognita*, the vast southern continent that mapmakers asserted for centuries to balance the globe and sailors kept half-finding, was an invitation, a placeholder shaped exactly like human curiosity. A data gap is a different kind of nothing.

Maybe that's why readers have always loved a map on the endpapers of a novel. Tolkien's Middle-earth, Le Guin's Earthsea: publishers learned long ago that a fantasy novel with a map in front is trusted in a way a mapless one isn't. The map is a promise that the place exists, that it has edges, that there is more of it than the story shows. Le Guin used to say Earthsea began with the islands, drawn before she knew who would live on them; the story was invented to explain the map, not the other way around. A map is the most economical form of world-building ever devised. One page of ink, and the reader's imagination supplies ten thousand unnamed villages.

---

Try an experiment tonight. Draw your neighborhood from memory: streets, corners, the things at the edges. It will be wrong, and the wrongness is the interesting part. What comes out large is what you love. What's missing is what you have never once noticed: the shape of the block you cross every day, the name of the street you turn onto without looking. The frayed edge, where your confident lines dissolve into white, is the world, waiting.

Every map puts something at the center. Hereford is candid about it: Christ at the top, Jerusalem in the middle, everything else arranged outward in declining order of significance. Our maps are shy about performing the same operation. The blue dot, the friendliest feature of the modern map, is at least honest: it puts you at the center and admits it. X marks the spot, and the spot is always "you are here."

The dragons were never at the edge of the world. They live five miles from your door, in the districts you've never entered, in the blank parts of the city you call home. Every one of us stands at the center of a map, and the only interesting question is how much of it we've walked.

**The Center of the World**

In Hereford Cathedral they keep a room deliberately dark, because what's in it is fragile and old and does not take light well. It is a map of the world, drawn around the year 1300 on a single calfskin: the largest medieval world map to survive, nearly five feet tall. The unknown draftsman put east at the top, because that's where the sun rises and where Eden was thought to sit. Christ reigns at the summit. Jerusalem occupies the exact center. Britain, where the map was made, is squeezed into the far-left margin like an afterthought. Noah's Ark rests on Ararat. The labyrinth of Crete coils in the Aegean. The Golden Fleece hangs in the Caucasus. And off in the south, in the margins of Africa, the monsters.

(~150 words)

The modern viewer's first instinct is to call it wrong. But "wrong" assumes it was attempting what our maps attempt and failing at it. It wasn't. It's a different genre entirely: an encyclopedia in the shape of the world, a sermon in the shape of the world. It doesn't measure miles; it measures importance. Places are drawn large because they matter. In that sense it is more honest than most maps we use, because its values are printed right on its surface, in gold, at the top. Even the word is humble about this: mappa meant cloth, napkin. The world, drawn on something the size of a tablecloth, at the scale of one family's dinner.

(~105)

---

All maps are arguments. Every map is a set of claims about what matters, and the louder claim is always about what doesn't: what got left out so the rest could be legible. The modern map hides its editorial hand behind the grid of latitude and longitude and the reassuring beige of continents, but the hand is there. Selection is not a defect that better technology will remove. The only map with no editorial hand is the territory itself, and it is useless as a map.

(~85)

Lewis Carroll saw the problem first. In "Sylvie and Bruno Concluded," a character boasts of his kingdom's map at a scale of a mile to a mile. The farmers object that it would cover the whole country and shut out the sunlight, and so the map is never spread out. Borges compressed the joke into a single paragraph, "On Exactitude in Science": an empire of perfect cartographers produces a map the size of the empire, point for point coincident with it, and later generations, less devoted, abandon it to the sun and rain. Cartography is the art of leaving things out. A good map is a betrayal so skillful you're grateful for it.

(~110)

---

You cannot flatten a sphere without lying. Geometry forbids it: the curvature of the earth cannot be pressed into a plane without something tearing or stretching. So every flat map chooses which truth to keep and which to abandon: area, shape, distance, or direction. Pick one.

Gerardus Mercator, in 1569, picked direction, because his customers were drowning. On a Mercator map a line of constant compass bearing, the line a ship actually holds when the helmsman keeps the needle steady, is straight. A navigator could put a ruler on the chart, draw a line from the Azores to the Caribbean, and steer it home. For this mercy the poles swell grotesquely: Greenland, a rough subcontinental icebox, looms on the classroom wall like a rival to Africa, which is in fact about fourteen times its size.

(~135)

The projection was built for the North Atlantic, and it flattered the North Atlantic. Then it escaped the ship and colonized the schoolroom, where its one talent, steering, was worthless and its distortion was dynamite. Generations of children absorbed the relative size of nations from it like fluoride in the water. The reckoning came in the 1970s, when Arno Peters promoted an equal-area projection as a corrective to centuries of visual imperialism; development agencies hung it in their lobbies, cartographers grumbled that his map mangled shapes and his history was shaky (the argument even got a scene in The West Wing), and the fight grew loud and moral and largely missed the point. The point is that every projection is a choice among lies. The only innocent map is a globe, and you can't fold a globe, file it, or hang it on a classroom wall. Convenience corrupts everything, including up. North-up is a habit, not a fact; an Australian named Stuart McArthur made this point in 1979 with his upside-down world map, Australia crowning the planet, and no one has ever produced an argument against it except habit.

(~185)

---

Maps don't merely describe power; sometimes they are the instrument of it. In 1930s America, federal appraisers drew maps of cities and graded the neighborhoods, and the worst grade, shaded red, was assigned where Black and immigrant families lived, and labeled "hazardous." Lenders steered capital around those districts for decades. The decline the map predicted, the map's readers produced. Red ink hardened into fact, into walls, into a geography of exclusion whose lines are still visible from above, in tree cover and life expectancy, in any American city you care to check. This is the uncomfortable energy in the word "cartography": naming a coast has always been a way of claiming it, and drawing a line has always been a way of making one.

(~120)

In 1933, London Transit published a map of the Underground designed by Harry Beck, an engineering draftsman who happened at the time to be out of work. Beck's insight was ruthless: nobody uses the Underground map to walk. A passenger needs to know sequence and interchange, not geography. So he threw geography away. Stations spaced evenly no matter the distance. Lines restricted to horizontal, vertical, and forty-five degrees. The Thames reduced to a single blue gesture. The story goes that he took the logic from electrical circuit diagrams, which don't care where the components physically sit either; the map was initially rejected, then tried in a pocket edition, and within a few years it was the mental furniture of an entire city.

(~120)

The city rearranged itself to match the diagram. Distances stretched and shrank in the popular imagination: central stations a few hundred meters apart look like expeditions, and tourists take taxis between them, while long suburban runs look like nothing at all. People chose flats by diagram logic. The map ate the territory. And Beck himself: a modest one-time fee, then four decades of submitting revisions while others signed the work, and recognition that arrived mostly after his death. It is among the most-seen British designs of the twentieth century, and its author spent his life trying to get his name back on it, which tells you something about how maps treat their makers, too.

(~110)

---

For most of history, being on a map was an achievement reserved for cities, rivers, coastlines, kings. People lived in the spaces between the labels. Now the average person spends the entire day as a moving blue point. The map no longer asks where you are; it tells you. An entire genre of small civic performance, the fingertip on the folded paper, the "you are here" sign at the trailhead, the stranger stopped on the corner and consulted like an oracle, has nearly gone extinct.

(~85)

The new maps argue in subtler voices. Open a map of Crimea in Moscow and the peninsula is solidly Russian; open it in Washington and it's dashed, contested, a question mark. One body of water carries different names depending on the nationality of your internet connection. In 2018, the fitness app Strava published a global heat map of its users' runs and rides, and analysts noticed bright rings of athletic activity around certain compounds in certain deserts, where soldiers had been jogging with their trackers on: the map of exercise became a map of secret infrastructure. And every time your phone hands you the "fastest route," someone's algorithm is deciding which streets deserve your presence, which shuttered storefronts you'll pass, which neighborhoods you will never see at all. We asked for the whole world in our pockets. What we got is a very persuasive opinion about it.

(~140)

The maps that matter most are unpublished. In 1960 an urban planner named Kevin Lynch asked people in Boston, Jersey City, and Los Angeles to sketch their cities from memory, and out of the wobbly, contradictory drawings he extracted the five elements of every mental map: paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks. Everyone's map is wrong in informative ways. Home is enormous. The commute is a trunk line, wide as a river. The district two miles away is blank as the open sea.

The navigators of the Marshall Islands made charts of sticks and cowrie shells, curved sticks representing the way ocean swells bend and interfere around atolls, shells marking the islands themselves: maps not of where things are but of how the sea behaves. That is the opposite of the blue dot, which never lets you graduate.

**The Center of the World**

In Hereford Cathedral they keep a room deliberately dark, because what's in it is fragile and old and does not take light well. It is a map of the world, drawn around the year 1300 on a single calfskin: the largest medieval world map to survive, nearly five feet tall. The unknown draftsman put east at the top, because that's where the sun rises and where Eden was thought to sit. Christ reigns at the summit. Jerusalem occupies the exact center. Britain, where the map was made, is squeezed into the far-left margin like an afterthought. Noah's Ark rests on Ararat. The labyrinth of Crete coils in the Aegean. The Golden Fleece hangs in the Caucasus. And off in the south, in the margins of Africa, the monsters.

(~150 words)

The modern viewer's first instinct is to call it wrong. But "wrong" assumes it was attempting what our maps attempt and failing at it. It wasn't. It's a different genre entirely: an encyclopedia in the shape of the world, a sermon in the shape of the world. It doesn't measure miles; it measures importance. Places are drawn large because they matter. In that sense it is more honest than most maps we use, because its values are printed right on its surface, in gold, at the top. Even the word is humble about this: mappa meant cloth, napkin. The world, drawn on something the size of a tablecloth, at the scale of one family's dinner.

(~105)

---

All maps are arguments. Every map is a set of claims about what matters, and the louder claim is always about what doesn't: what got left out so the rest could be legible. The modern map hides its editorial hand behind the grid of latitude and longitude and the reassuring beige of continents, but the hand is there. Selection is not a defect that better technology will remove. The only map with no editorial hand is the territory itself, and it is useless as a map.

(~85)

Lewis Carroll saw the problem first. In "Sylvie and Bruno Concluded," a character boasts of his kingdom's map at a scale of a mile to a mile. The farmers object that it would cover the whole country and shut out the sunlight, and so the map is never spread out. Borges compressed the joke into a single paragraph, "On Exactitude in Science": an empire of perfect cartographers produces a map the size of the empire, point for point coincident with it, and later generations, less devoted, abandon it to the sun and rain. Cartography is the art of leaving things out. A good map is a betrayal so skillful you're grateful for it.

(~110)

---

You cannot flatten a sphere without lying. Geometry forbids it: the curvature of the earth cannot be pressed into a plane without something tearing or stretching. So every flat map chooses which truth to keep and which to abandon: area, shape, distance, or direction. Pick one.

Gerardus Mercator, in 1569, picked direction, because his customers were drowning. On a Mercator map a line of constant compass bearing, the line a ship actually holds when the helmsman keeps the needle steady, is straight. A navigator could put a ruler on the chart, draw a line from the Azores to the Caribbean, and steer it home. For this mercy the poles swell grotesquely: Greenland, a rough subcontinental icebox, looms on the classroom wall like a rival to Africa, which is in fact about fourteen times its size.

(~135)

The projection was built for the North Atlantic, and it flattered the North Atlantic. Then it escaped the ship and colonized the schoolroom, where its one talent, steering, was worthless and its distortion was dynamite. Generations of children absorbed the relative size of nations from it like fluoride in the water. The reckoning came in the 1970s, when Arno Peters promoted an equal-area projection as a corrective to centuries of visual imperialism; development agencies hung it in their lobbies, cartographers grumbled that his map mangled shapes and his history was shaky (the argument even got a scene in The West Wing), and the fight grew loud and moral and largely missed the point. The point is that every projection is a choice among lies. The only innocent map is a globe, and you can't fold a globe, file it, or hang it on a classroom wall. Convenience corrupts everything, including up. North-up is a habit, not a fact; an Australian named Stuart McArthur made this point in 1979 with his upside-down world map, Australia crowning the planet, and no one has ever produced an argument against it except habit.

(~185)

---

Maps don't merely describe power; sometimes they are the instrument of it. In 1930s America, federal appraisers drew maps of cities and graded the neighborhoods, and the worst grade, shaded red, was assigned where Black and immigrant families lived, and labeled "hazardous." Lenders steered capital around those districts for decades. The decline the map predicted, the map's readers produced. Red ink hardened into fact, into walls, into a geography of exclusion whose lines are still visible from above, in tree cover and life expectancy, in any American city you care to check. This is the uncomfortable energy in the word "cartography": naming a coast has always been a way of claiming it, and drawing a line has always been a way of making one.

(~120)

---

In 1933, London Transit published a map of the Underground designed by Harry Beck, an engineering draftsman who happened at the time to be out of work. Beck's insight was ruthless: nobody uses the Underground map to walk. A passenger needs to know sequence and interchange, not geography. So he threw geography away. Stations spaced evenly no matter the distance. Lines restricted to horizontal, vertical, and forty-five degrees. The Thames reduced to a single blue gesture. The story goes that he took the logic from electrical circuit diagrams, which don't care where the components physically sit either; the map was initially rejected, then tried in a pocket edition, and within a few years it was the mental furniture of an entire city.

(~120)

The city rearranged itself to match the diagram. Distances stretched and shrank in the popular imagination: central stations a few hundred meters apart look like expeditions, and tourists take taxis between them, while long suburban runs look like nothing at all. People chose flats by diagram logic. The map ate the territory. And Beck himself: a modest one-time fee, then four decades of submitting revisions while others signed the work, and recognition that arrived mostly after his death. It is among the most-seen British designs of the twentieth century, and its author spent his life trying to get his name back on it, which tells you something about how maps treat their makers, too.

(~110)

---

For most of history, being on a map was an achievement reserved for cities, rivers, coastlines, kings. People lived in the spaces between the labels. Now the average person spends the entire day as a moving blue point. The map no longer asks where you are; it tells you. An entire genre of small civic performance, the fingertip on the folded paper, the "you are here" sign at the trailhead, the stranger stopped on the corner and consulted like an oracle, has nearly gone extinct.

(~85)

The new maps argue in subtler voices. Open a map of Crimea in Moscow and the peninsula is solidly Russian; open it in Washington and it's dashed, contested, a question mark. One body of water carries different names depending on the nationality of your internet connection. In 2018, the fitness app Strava published a global heat map of its users' runs and rides, and analysts noticed bright rings of athletic activity around certain compounds in certain deserts, where soldiers had been jogging with their trackers on: the map of exercise became a map of secret infrastructure. And every time your phone hands you the "fastest route," someone's algorithm is deciding which streets deserve your presence, which shuttered storefronts you'll pass, which neighborhoods you will never see at all. We asked for the whole world in our pockets. What we got is a very persuasive opinion about it.

(~140)

---

The maps that matter most are unpublished. In 1960 an urban planner named Kevin Lynch asked people in Boston, Jersey City, and Los Angeles to sketch their cities from memory, and out of the wobbly, contradictory drawings he extracted the five elements of every mental map: paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks. Everyone's map is wrong in informative ways. Home is enormous. The commute is a trunk line, wide as a river. The district two miles away is blank as the open sea.

(~90)

Ask someone for directions and you receive a fragment of autobiography. "Left where the video store used to be." "It's past the good bakery, not the disappointing one." We navigate by demolished buildings. Our mental maps are of time as much as space, layered palimpsests of every city we've lived in, and the person giving directions is reading off a map no one else can see, of a city that partially no longer exists. As for "here be dragons": the phrase, famously, appears essentially once in the entire history of cartography, on a small bronze globe from around 1510 now in the New York Public Library. But the condition it names is real and everyone has one: unexplored water inside the harbor, the neighborhood five miles from your door that you have never once entered, though you have flown over other continents.

(~135)

Not all maps even map land. The navigators of the Marshall Islands made charts of sticks and cowrie shells, curved sticks representing the way ocean swells bend and interfere around atolls, shells marking the islands themselves: maps not of where things are but of how the sea behaves. And many of these charts were meant to be memorized and then left on shore. Success was measured by how completely you could stop needing the map. That is the opposite of the blue dot, which never lets you graduate.

(~90)

---

And some things are still blank. Only about a quarter of the ocean floor has been mapped to modern resolution; we have better maps of Mars, and of the Moon, than of the majority of our own planet's surface. The nearest alien world is under the keel. There is an effort underway, Seabed 2030, to finish the job, and it should be finished. But it's worth noticing what a blank used to be. Terra Australis Incognita, the vast southern continent that mapmakers asserted for centuries to balance the globe and sailors kept half-finding, was an invitation, a placeholder shaped exactly like human curiosity. A data gap is a different kind of nothing.

Try an experiment tonight. Draw your neighborhood from memory: streets, corners, the things at the edges. It will be wrong, and the wrongness is the interesting part. What comes out large is what you love. What's missing is what you have never once noticed: the shape of the block you cross every day, the name of the street you turn onto without looking. The frayed edge, where your confident lines dissolve into white, is the world, waiting.

(~75)

Every map puts something at the center. The Hereford map is candid about it: Christ at the top, Jerusalem in the middle, everything else arranged outward in declining order of significance. Our maps are shy about the same operation. The blue dot, the friendliest feature of the modern map, is at least honest: it puts you at the center and admits it. X marks the spot, and the spot is always "you are here."
